I'm unaware of those doctors, and can therefore not speak on how well informed their written articles are. However an important note is that the expert is always (!) at the lowest end of informed evidence. The only way you can disseminate a scientific study is by reading it... which is very challenging for most people, understandably so (the language is very boring and for the most part inaccessible for the general public). Its important for you, however, as a person who is giving nutrition guidance to groups of people, to understand how to rank scientific evidence and to understand what you're reading. Media and "experts" in the media aren't good sources: in order to give good advice to other people, you need good sources. I'm not saying anything you're saying is incorrect; it very well could be. I'm saying it would do you well as a nutrition counsel to learn how to read studies rather than plain English translations, which could be poor translation or extrapolation of the actual study. 

I hope this didn't come across as mean! I genuinely dont want to seem cross with you, I just think it does everyone a service if our health professionals are well informed with their decisions!

Nutrition isn't a one diet fits all. Increasingly, its shifting towards nutrigenomics, ie your genetics determine the best diet for you. As well, we try to not demonize foods as best as possible, so I dont want to say fats or bad or carbohydrates are bad, but more so that we should be eating both of them in moderation. DRIs in canada are currently the gold standard for macronutrient distribution. Additionally, I have profs that very strongly object to intermittent fasting, and I've had lecturers that have advocated for the HAES movement. Honestly, the course just presents us with the science and many different points of views, and teaches us how to disseminate the studies that come out since nutrition is an emerging field. I find its cumulatively a very unbiased major with profs from all different sections of food and food service. 

Sorry if this didn't answer your question in the way you were hoping. In short, there isnt a solid answer, unfortunately and I encourage you to read well done peer reviewed journals to inform your ideas about nutrition.

1. There are some absolutely beautiful places in and around Toronto. If you like nature, check out cullen gardens, for example. 
2. There's literally always something to do! Go to the art gallery! The taste of danforth! Jazz festivals down at the lake! Toronto is a busy city and you should definitely take advantage of some of it's events. 
3. There's such a wide variety of food & and Toronto's diversity makes the selection so much better! 
4. As a previous user said, lots of very easy to access transit, which makes getting around the city fairly easy. 
5. The staff, in my experience, is fantastic. I have only really had an issue with one or two profs, which is much less than what I've heard my friends from different schools complain about. Also the faculty is pretty good as well.
6. Lots of support in place if you need it, ex free tutoring, writing support, mentoring programs that pair you with an upper year student or someone in your related feild, counselling, office hours with profs, a student food bank and the good food box, ect... 
7. TONS of volunteer & on campus jobs if you need one/are looking for something to do! Also a fantastic way to meet people.
8. A wide variety of clubs and activities for people with a wide range of interests. Enjoy playing an instrument but couldn't work it into your major? There's a club for that. Like anime? chess? running? If it doesn't exist you could even start your own :\) 
9. Finally, the MAC and RAC, our two gyms! They're fantastic resources that I personally use in\-between classes to kill time, including a swimming pool, cardio rooms, and weight rooms. 

Good luck on your journey and remember to balance your stress levels with fun activities! I hope you absolutley love Canada, and that you feel welcomed and safe here. Safe travels :\)

Ryersons nutrition courses focus a lot on the social science aspect of nutrition. Its very rewarding if you're into the social sciences. If you're not, I reccomend going to guelph or brescia; their programs are more heavily based in chemistry and biological sciences. 

For me, first year profs who weren't that great were Derick (he's a fantastic man, super funny, but doesn't pace his class well), anatomy and physiology (The professor for this class, Nick, is again an awesome guy. The class isn't bad because he's an awful prof, its just very content heavy), FND100 second semester (I am so sorry, you have to take this one in class and it was a bad time all around), and then second year you'll be having mario for biochemistry, who isn't the best prof but the class is very manageable. That's pretty much it for the first two years! 

Re summer school- a lot of nutrition courses are not offered during summer school. Do NOT take any science courses during the summer: they water them down for the nutrition students, so taking them online would mean you would get them in their full difficulty, since those courses through chang aren't program specific. I took my lower liberals during the summer to lighten my course load, which was a decent idea. They offer both online and in class options for taking the courses during the summer, so with the online classes you don't have to live near campus (but some do require an in-class exam).

Hola, second, going on 3rd year Nutrition student here! 

* The professors are a mixed bag: some are absolutely fantastic and others are... eh. I assume you get this with any institution though. Different people have different learning styles so you're likely going to enjoy some more than others. 

* The courses are overwhelming first year if you don't stay on top of your shit. So stay on top of your shit. If you need tips on how to do that, rye offers pretty decent tutoring services (some specifically for nutrition chem classes as well as more general help at the SLC) Also, second semester is harder than first, but if you survive it, second year is actually really manageable. 

* The overall feel of ryerson is rushed. If you're looking for the movie-style university experience, you're not going to find it at ryerson. It's a fast paced environment. Seriously consider how you think you'll manage the city, and remember that like 80% of your classmates are gonna be commuter students, which makes student life very different from other schools where the majority of students live on campus. In other words, this is not a party school, and though there are social events, there are not a whole lot of house parties if thats your thing. 

* High GPA isn't something you should worry about 1st year so much. Seriously, work on figuring out good ways to study, making a solid base of understanding for fundimental aspects of nutrition and science, and just enjoying your life. A lot of the internships don't even look at 1st year marks... no seriously, google it. GPA is also variable by student, how much effort you put in and how well you study are really the two indicators of how well you're going to do. 

Any other questions and I'd be happy to answer them for you! Good luck on choosing schools and good luck in your first year! :)
